pr_title: drivers: flash: spi_nor: make page size and erase sizes configurable
pr_body:
JEDEC compatible spi nor devices are not required to have a
standard page and sector size as well as supported erase sizes. The
JEDEC SFDP headers supports up to four erase types with configurable
size and op-code.
Make page size and erase types configurable by adding properties for
the corresponding DWORDS from the JEDEC Basic Flash Parameter Table,
documented in JESD216B. The defaults reflect the drivers old behaviour.

Remove has-be32k property because it is never read.

Fixes  #23322
Fixes  #23673

Signed-off-by: Thomas Schmid <tom@lfence.de>
pr_comments:
**All checks are passing now.**

Resolved conflicts with master. The changes that we discussed earlier are already incorporated:

- Erase type and page size encoding by JESD216B DWORD
- Simple search for the most suitable erase size (see spi_nor_select_erase_type())

@galak and @pabigot: Would you mind reviewing again?

Tagged dev-review to discuss @galak's NAK, particularly the removal of defaults from the binding file which is burdensome and would break out-of-tree devicetrees.  I'd like this in v2.3, so marking it for that too.
Thank you for the review and comments @pabigot.

@galak No, I'm mostly concerned that we'd be forcing people to add a rather opaque set of property values when we can provide a default that matches the existing behavior.  To do so would break all out-of-tree devicetree specifications that have been working since spi-nor was added (and all in-tree specifications would have to be updated in this PR).

> @galak No, I'm mostly concerned that we'd be forcing people to add a rather opaque set of property values when we can provide a default that matches the existing behavior. To do so would break all out-of-tree devicetree specifications that have been working since spi-nor was added (and all in-tree specifications would have to be updated in this PR).

So I get that concern.  But how generic are these property values?  I'm concerned the out-of-tree cases break because they are using the defaults and they aren't aware they need to change things.

> So I get that concern. But how generic are these property values? I'm concerned the out-of-tree cases break because they are using the defaults and they aren't aware they need to change things.

The defaults encode the erase support and page size that were hard-coded before.  They're as generic as we can get.

There is a means to provide defaults in the driver code w/o the YAML support.  You can do something like:

```
COND_CODE_1(DT_INST_NODE_HAS_PROP(0, sfdp_basic_8), (DT_INST_PROP(0, sfdp_basic_8)), (0xD810200C))
```

> There is a means to provide defaults in the driver code w/o the YAML support.

Why would we hide the default value deep in a macro substitution in the driver implementation when Zephyr's binding description follows DT-Schema and [explicitly supports](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/44e2a0343d7ba804fb7e9f7673455bcba6935014/dts/binding-template.yaml#L207) putting it in the binding file, where it documents the sort of value that's expected to be supplied and incidently provides that value when the property isn't overridden in the devicetree source.

I understand you don't like the default feature, but it's there specifically to support this sort of situation.  If you want it removed please create an RFC proposal so we can discuss it.  I can see an argument for changing it to be informational and have no effect on the generated bindings, but until that's agreed on we should be allowed to use existing functionality.

issue_context.title: spi-nor driver fails to check for support of 32 KiBy block erase
issue_context.body:
The devicetree bindings were updated to add support for `has-be32k` which indicates a chip supports an optional 32 KiBy block erase, but the code doesn't verify that the specific instance has confirmed support for the command.  Consequently erases of sizes in the range `[32768, 65536)` may fail on some devices.

This would be fixed in #23658, but if that doesn't get in it'll need to be fixed separately.

review_comments: The MT25Q supposedly has this feature but the command is not 0xC7 (it's 0xC4).  I recall there was some question as to whether it functionally required iterating through the multiple dies on the chip, so it's fine to ignore it for now.

The die erase cmd has different structure than chip erase. It requires an address with the command. One solution, although a dirty hack, would be to specify 0xC4 as forth erase size and disable chip erase. I would prefer to ignore it until we have a better understanding of multi die devices in general.

I'm intrigued that these seem to differ from what linux has for the opcodes in `include/linux/mtd/spi-nor.h`:

specifically that `0x20` was defined as `SPINOR_OP_BE_4K` and `0xD8` as `SPINOR_OP_SE`

To some degree this is detritus.

What we're calling "JEDEC SPI-NOR" really isn't a standard; see commit comment of bb106390a29af81716ec89c0ae1be4e91dca69aa.  AFAIK none of these commands are formally standardized.

The M25P80 reference device, which Linux follows, uses 0xD8 for "sector erase" (sector = 512 KiBi = 64 KiBy), and 0xC7 for "bulk erase" (8 MiBi = 1 MiBy).  Those are the only erase commands supported in that device.  The concept of "block" in that device is limited to write protection of groups of sectors.

Later chips provided a smaller erasable unit (4 KiBy) and repurposed the term "sector" for that (probably based on disk file system terminology), calling the 64 KiBy unit a "block".  Even later, vendors supported a half-block (32 KiBy) unit.

The Winbond W25Q family was the primary target for the first instance of the driver in 87e54931670aabd6a6f69f773073d21cba72202c.  Its datasheet documents 0x20 as the "sector  erase" command where "sector" is 4 KiBy, and has "64 KiBy block erase" and "32 KiBy block erase" commands at 0xD8 and 0x52 respectively.  Generally devices have supported 4 KiBy and 64 KiBy erase commands, with some adding a 32 KiBy one.  Now we're finding devices that don't support any of these.

So that's history.  Much of the unending pain of maintaining this module has been related to slowly backing away from these hard-coded size/command associations.
Huh.  `has-be32k` was supposed to gate use of `SPI_NOR_BLOCK32_SIZE`.  My bad.
